newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar surges in Tokyo, seen pushing higher.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surges in Tokyo, seen pushing higher.

text.p: The dollar soared over two yen in Tokyo on Wednesday to a fresh four-year high as a belief grew that the big financial powers would not block its rise.
The rally gave a boost to Japanese stocks by triggering a blue-chip buying spree.

The weaker yen set investors hunting for Japanese exporters like Sony Corp and Toyota Motor Corp, which will gain from the dollar's increased purchasing power, pushing up the key Nikkei share index by three percent.
The Nikkei average of 225 leading shares jumped 538.73 points, or 3.03 percent, to close at 18,335.30. Its March futures rose 580 points to 18,370.

A dollar rally in U.S. trading on Tuesday picked up steam in Tokyo, with institutional buying pushing the greenback as high as 122.75 yen in late-afternoon trade, its highest point since February 1993, dealers said.

The dollar has been surging on the relative strength of the U.S. economy and signs that the big financial powers are prepared to tolerate its advance. Dealers said the dollar could scale fresh heights. "There are no real barriers," one said.

Extra fuel was added to the rise in overseas trade with the release of benign U.S. inflation data and fresh signals that the "Group of Three" nations -- the United States, Germany and Japan -- would not stand in the dollar's way.
The dollar finished at about 121 yen in U.S. trade on Tuesday after surging to a peak of 121.75 yen during the day.

Fears of dollar-selling intervention by the Bank of Japan (BOJ), which had been limiting the rise, mostly faded after a Japanese Finance Ministry official said on Tuesday that the yen's recent slide was not a cause for immediate concern.
On Wednesday, a senior Japanese Finance Ministry official, Kosuke Nakahira, told Reuters Japan needed to keep close watch on currency moves because there were signs they could speed up.
Nakahira, a special adviser to the finance minister, added that wild swings were not good for business as they could lead to a loss of confidence in a currency.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was quoted by Jiji news agency as saying on Wednesday that he did not welcome rapid changes in foreign-exchange levels, although he added that recent moves reflected the dollar's strength.
Neither of these comments stood in the dollar's way.
The currency was pushed rapidly higher by a broad dollar buying spree joined by securities firms which had held back from buying previously, as well as by trust banks and U.S. funds.
On the stock market, a surge in interest in export-orientated multinationals drove the key Nikkei average back to above 18,000 for the first time since last Thursday.
"After the Nikkei 225 rose above 18,000, buying gathered momentum," said Sueharu Ando, head of the equity trading division at Nikko Securities Co Ltd.
Although a weak yen can help exporters by making their products more competitive overseas, it can also encourage foreign investors to sell Japanese shares as their value in dollar terms ebbs away.
The market, battered in recent sessions by worries over the economy and the health of the banking sector, chose to take the weaker yen as a plus for exporters, the broker said.
Sony rose 260 yen to close at 8,250 yen, while Toyota also firmed by 20 yen to 3,230 yen in hefty turnover of 7.85 million shares.
